summary: Updates DCCP by adding the DCCP-Listen packet, helping applications connect through middleboxes like NATs and when a DCCP server sits behind one. It supports a simultaneous-open technique, in which both ends start the connection at once.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people behind locked gates both reach out at the same moment, so they meet in the middle. This adds the signal needed to let that happen.

questions: how does dccp work through a nat
what are the dccp invited and listen1 states
subtitle: Adds the DCCP-Listen packet so a DCCP server behind a NAT or firewall can punch a hole and let a client connect.

tldr.problem: DCCP servers wait passively for connection requests, but a server behind a NAPT or firewall that only allows outbound-initiated traffic cannot be reached by a client.
tldr.mechanism: A server that knows its one client in advance sends a DCCP-Listen packet toward it, which creates state in the server's middlebox, and then waits for the client's DCCP-Request to arrive through that opening.
tldr.outcome: A DCCP client can connect to a server inside a middlebox without a relay server. The RFC updates RFC 4340, adds two server states (INVITED and LISTEN1) and registers packet type 10.

today: RFC 5596 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4340. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Passive Servers
sections.content:
The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340) is both datagram-based and connection-oriented. DCCP servers wait passively for connection requests that DCCP clients send actively. That asymmetry causes trouble when the server sits inside a middlebox such as a Network Address Port Translator (NAPT) that only lets connection requests start from the inside. Host-based and network firewalls can behave the same way, and the RFC notes this is the default for many firewalls.

UDP can traverse middleboxes with techniques that rely on it being connectionless, and TCP uses its simultaneous-open procedure. The ideas behind the TCP solution apply to DCCP, but DCCP cannot just reuse the same methods. Appendix A explains that TCP simultaneous-open erases the client/server distinction, while DCCP features such as feature negotiation and the closing states rely on clear roles.

The RFC considers three cases: a private client reaching a public server, a public client reaching a private server, and a private client reaching a private server. The first already works with RFC 4340. This document supports the second and third without a DCCP relay server. It requires the server to learn the client's IP address and DCCP port out of band, for example with the Session Description Protocol (SDP).
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a server just waits for visitors. But if the server is behind a gate that only opens for people it has already contacted, no visitor can get in until the server reaches out first.

sections.title: The DCCP-Listen Packet
sections.content:
The update adds one new packet type, DCCP-Listen, with the DCCP generic header followed by a Service Code. Its format matches a DCCP-Request; only the Type value differs. IANA assigned Type 10 to it.

  • Source Port is the port on which the server is listening for a connection from the client's address. Dest Port is the port the client chose, which must be communicated to the server out of band.
  • X MUST be 1, because no connection exists yet to negotiate short sequence numbers. CCVal and CsCov MUST be zero, and Data Offset MUST be five or more (at least 20 bytes).
  • The Sequence Number is unrelated to normal DCCP sequence numbers. A server SHOULD set it to 0, a client MUST ignore it, and middleboxes MUST NOT interpret it.
  • Service Code MUST match a Service Code the server is really offering for that source address and port. It also has to be told to the server out of band beforehand.
  • Options and payload data MUST be ignored. Feature values cannot be negotiated with this packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The DCCP-Listen packet is a tiny note that says "I am here, ready for you." It looks like a normal connection request, but nobody is supposed to read much into the numbers inside it.

sections.title: Server and Client Behaviour
sections.content:
A server that does not know its client in advance keeps the existing RFC 4340 path (CLOSED, LISTEN, RESPOND). The new behaviour applies to a fully specified server endpoint, one that permits exactly one client, identified by IP address and port, plus a single Service Code. Such a server SHOULD send a DCCP-Listen from CLOSED and enter the new INVITED state.

While in INVITED the server SHOULD repeat the DCCP-Listen every 200 milliseconds, at most 2 repetitions. If it is still in INVITED 200 ms after the third DCCP-Listen, it SHOULD move to the second new state, LISTEN1, which waits passively and sends no more Listen packets. A DCCP-Request in either state leads to RESPOND. ICMP errors received in reply to a DCCP-Listen SHOULD be treated as soft errors that cause no state change.

Servers SHOULD ignore incoming DCCP-Listen packets, and MAY answer one with a DCCP-Reset (Code 7, Connection Refused), which signals that two servers are waiting on the same port.

A client MUST silently discard any DCCP-Listen it receives. There is one optional optimisation: a client in the REQUEST state MAY immediately retransmit its DCCP-Request on the first DCCP-Listen, treated like a timeout, and it MUST do this only once per connection. Routers and middleboxes should forward DCCP-Listen packets end to end. Middleboxes may use the address, port and Service Code in them to create forwarding state, and NAT handling is covered in RFC 5597.
sections.plainLanguage: The server knocks on the gate up to three times, 200 milliseconds apart. After that it just waits quietly. If the client's request shows up at any point, the server answers it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the RFC's examples DCCP A is the client and DCCP B is the server. Each sits behind a middlebox (NA and NB) that lets outgoing DCCP packets through but only admits incoming ones when a matching packet has already gone out.

When the server starts first, its DCCP-Listen leaves through NB, which creates the hole. NA drops that packet because it has no hole yet. The client then sends a DCCP-Request, which passes NB's new opening, and the server replies with a DCCP-Response. Both middleboxes now have state, so the handshake completes and data flows.

If the DCCP-Request is lost, the server repeats the Listen, and after the third timer expiry it enters LISTEN1 to wait for a late or retransmitted request. In the triggered-retransmission example, a lost first Listen and a lost Request are repaired when the retransmitted Listen prompts the client to resend the Request. If Listen and Request cross, the server may see two Requests and send a second, unnecessary Response, which the client ignores in PARTOPEN. The RFC expects this not to modify or delay the open procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The server's knock opens its own gate. Then the client's message follows the same path in, and the two can talk. If a knock gets lost, the server simply knocks again.

sections.title: Design Choices and Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC explains why a new packet type was used instead of reusing DCCP-Request. Overloading DCCP-Request would force hosts and stateful middleboxes to have two processing paths for one packet. A client could answer a server's Request with a DCCP-Reset or DCCP-Sync, and a DCCP-SyncAck would not be meaningful before initial sequence numbers exist. A separate type keeps processing simpler and clearer.

The timing is deliberate. Repeats must be spaced far enough apart to avoid correlated loss, and the 200 ms interval was chosen to suit a wide range of wireless and wired paths. Middleboxes need to see a Listen before the DCCP-Request times out at 1 second. Three transmissions at 200 ms spacing total 600 ms, which stays below that. Moving to LISTEN1 afterwards lets any late Request still reach the server.

Listen packets are sent only when the endpoint is fully specified, so ordinary connections are unaffected. A client that conforms to this document works with an RFC 4340 server, and an RFC 4340-only client ignores a DCCP-Listen, which is also the behaviour required here. The authors expect no practical deployment problems.
sections.plainLanguage: They made a brand-new kind of knock instead of reusing the old one, so nobody mistakes a knock for a real request. The knocks are spaced out so one bad moment does not lose all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A DCCP-Listen exposes that a server is passively waiting for a known client. It is not encrypted, so an on-path attacker could see it and spoof a DCCP-Request or DCCP-Reset using the matching addresses, ports and Service Code, to inject data or deny the connection. The RFC notes a similar on-path attack is possible for any DCCP connection once the client starts it.

Because the exchange relies on out-of-band signaling, the Listen is only sent after explicit prior signaling from the client. The method also forces the server to hold state for a connection not yet established, which the RFC calls a change in DCCP's security profile, with expected minimal impact. A client only responds to a Listen whose server address and port match an existing connection in the REQUEST state, so the method cannot redirect a connection to a different server.

Servers SHOULD permit generating DCCP-Listen by default. A server that wants to avoid disclosing this information MAY skip it, possibly inhibiting middlebox traversal.
sections.plainLanguage: Knocking tells anyone watching the road that the server is waiting. That is a small risk, so a server can choose not to knock, but then the gate might stay shut.

fields.desc: Port on which the server is listening.

fields.name: Dest Port
fields.desc: Port chosen by the client, communicated out of band.

fields.name: Sequence Number High Bits
fields.desc: Server SHOULD set to 0; clients ignore.

fields.desc: Server SHOULD set to 0; clients ignore.

fields.desc: Service the server is listening for.
